title: Where does the Spring Framework (and the JDK) already use GoF design patterns — Factory (BeanFactory/ApplicationContext), Singleton (default bean scope), Proxy (AOP, @Transactional, lazy beans), Template Method (JdbcTemplate/RestTemplate/JmsTemplate), Strategy (pluggable AuthenticationProviders, Resource loaders), Observer (ApplicationEvent/@EventListener), Decorator (BeanPostProcessor, servlet wrappers), Adapter (HandlerAdapter), Builder (UriComponentsBuilder), and in the JDK (Iterator, Comparator as Strategy, decorated java.io streams, Runnable/Callable) — and why does recognizing these show practical pattern understanding?
shortTitle: Where does Spring and the JDK already use GoF design patterns

s1_definition.profdef: The Spring Framework and the Java Development Kit are themselves built out of GoF design patterns, so every time you use Spring or the standard library you are already using patterns whether you name them or not. Spring's container is a Factory that creates and manages beans, beans are Singletons by default, AOP and @Transactional work through dynamic Proxies, the template classes like JdbcTemplate use Template Method, and events use Observer. The JDK uses Iterator for collections, treats Comparator as a Strategy, and decorates I/O streams. Recognizing these shows you understand patterns as living engineering tools, not textbook trivia.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's software is like the bank building itself. The container that hires and manages every employee for the whole bank is the Factory. Each manager role has exactly one person on duty — that is the Singleton. When a customer meets a "manager," they are often actually meeting a stand-in who checks their ID and logs the visit before passing them through — that stand-in is the Proxy, exactly how @Transactional works. Rajesh does not build any of this; it is already wired into the building he walks into.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spring and the JDK are patterns in disguise — Factory for beans, Singleton scope, Proxy for @Transactional, Template Method for JdbcTemplate, Observer for events, and Iterator plus Strategy throughout the JDK.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Spring Framework and the Java Development Kit are themselves built out of GoF design patterns, so every time you use Spring or the standard library you are already using patterns whether you name them or not. Spring's container is a Factory that creates and manages beans, beans are Singletons by default, AOP and @Transactional work through dynamic Proxies, the template classes like JdbcTemplate use Template Method, and events use Observer. The JDK uses Iterator for collections, treats Comparator as a Strategy, and decorates I/O streams. Recognizing these shows you understand patterns as living engineering tools, not textbook trivia.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's software is like the bank building itself. The container that hires and manages every employee for the whole bank is the Factory. Each manager role has exactly one person on duty — that is the Singleton. When a customer meets a "manager," they are often actually meeting a stand-in who checks their ID and logs the visit before passing them through — that stand-in is the Proxy, exactly how @Transactional works. Rajesh does not build any of this; it is already wired into the building he walks into.

**One line to remember:** Spring and the JDK are patterns in disguise — Factory for beans, Singleton scope, Proxy for @Transactional, Template Method for JdbcTemplate, Observer for events, and Iterator plus Strategy throughout the JDK.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring's `ApplicationContext` and `BeanFactory` are a textbook Factory. You ask the container for a bean and it decides how to construct it, wire its dependencies, and hand it back: `TransferService svc = context.getBean(TransferService.class)`. You never call `new TransferService(...)`, so the creation detail is centralized, which is exactly the Factory intent.

By default every Spring bean is a Singleton within the container. There is one shared `TransferService` instance for the whole application. This is Spring's own managed Singleton, distinct from the classic static Singleton, and it is why stateless services are the norm.

Spring AOP, `@Transactional`, and lazy beans all use the Proxy pattern. When you annotate a method with `@Transactional`, Spring does not inject your raw class; it injects a proxy that opens a transaction, calls your method, then commits or rolls back. For example `@Transactional public void transfer(...)` becomes a proxy that wraps your transfer with begin and commit logic.

The template classes use Template Method. `JdbcTemplate`, `RestTemplate`, and `JmsTemplate` define the fixed skeleton — acquire connection, run work, handle exceptions, release connection — and let you fill the one varying step through a callback: `jdbcTemplate.query(sql, (rs, i) -> new Account(rs.getString("id"), rs.getBigDecimal("balance")))`. The RowMapper you pass is the variable step.

Strategy shows up where behavior is pluggable. Spring Security picks among many `AuthenticationProvider` implementations at runtime; Spring's `Resource` loaders choose how to load a classpath versus a URL resource. In the JDK, `Comparator` is the clearest Strategy: `list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Account::getBalance))` swaps the sorting algorithm's comparison without touching the sort itself.

Observer appears as Spring's `ApplicationEvent` and `@EventListener`. You publish an event and every listener reacts: `publisher.publishEvent(new TransferCompletedEvent(id))`, and an audit listener annotated with `@EventListener` fires automatically.

Decorator shows up in `BeanPostProcessor`, which wraps beans to add behavior, and in servlet request/response wrappers. In the JDK, `java.io` is the canonical Decorator: `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f)))` layers buffering over decoding over raw bytes.

Adapter appears as Spring MVC's `HandlerAdapter`, which lets the dispatcher invoke many kinds of handlers through one interface. Builder appears as `UriComponentsBuilder.fromUriString("/api").queryParam("id", 1).build()`. And the JDK's `Iterator`, returned by every collection, is the Iterator pattern, while `Runnable` and `Callable` are Command objects.

The senior point: naming these proves you understand patterns operationally. You are not memorizing the GoF book; you are reading real frameworks fluently and can reason about why @Transactional sometimes fails on self-invocation (because the proxy is bypassed).
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India runs a Spring Boot transfer service, and the architect wants new joiners to see that the framework they use every day is made of patterns.

Problem 1 — Where do service objects come from? Nobody writes `new TransferService()`. The object simply appears, fully wired. The reason is the Spring container acting as a Factory, creating and injecting beans. New engineers must understand this so they stop trying to construct services manually.

Problem 2 — Why does a transfer either fully happen or fully roll back? The transfer method is annotated `@Transactional`, and a Proxy wraps it to open and commit the transaction. If a junior calls a `@Transactional` method from another method in the same class, the proxy is bypassed and the transaction silently does not start. Understanding the Proxy pattern explains this real bug.

Problem 3 — Why does the audit log appear without the transfer code calling it? Because the transfer publishes an event and an audit listener observes it. That is the Observer pattern, and recognizing it lets engineers add new reactions without editing transfer logic.

The demo is a small standalone program that mimics these behaviors in plain Java so the patterns are visible without needing a running Spring context: a tiny Factory for services, a hand-written transactional Proxy, a Template Method for database work, a Comparator Strategy, and an event publisher Observer.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.50,000 from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), then a query of two accounts.

Step 1: The MiniContainer is asked twice for a TransferService. The Factory logic builds the object the first time and caches it, so both requests return the exact same instance. The log confirms Singleton behavior — this mirrors Spring's default bean scope.

Step 2: TransactionalProxy.wrap wraps the raw service in a dynamic proxy. The returned reference looks like a TransferService but is actually a stand-in. This mirrors how @Transactional injects a proxy, not your raw class.

Step 3: Two listeners subscribe to the EventPublisher. They sit idle in a list until an event arrives. This is the Observer wiring, like registering @EventListener beans.

Step 4: `service.transfer(...)` is called on the proxy. The proxy logs BEGIN TX, then invokes the real method, then logs COMMIT TX. Inside the real method, the publisher fires, and both the audit and SMS listeners react. The transfer code itself never mentions audit or SMS.

Step 5: MiniJdbcTemplate.query runs. The template owns the fixed skeleton of fetching rows; the RowMapper lambda you passed is the one variable step that turns each raw row into an Account. This is Template Method plus a Strategy callback, exactly like JdbcTemplate with a RowMapper.

Step 6: The account list is sorted with `Comparator.comparing(Account::getBalance)`. The sort algorithm stays fixed; only the comparison strategy is swapped in. This is Strategy from the JDK.

Step 7: Each account is logged in ascending balance order. Every step used a different framework pattern, proving the framework is patterns under the hood.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Singleton? same instance = true
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] BEGIN TX transfer
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] AUDIT : TRANSFER SAV2001->CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] SMS   : Dear Rajesh, TRANSFER SAV2001->CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] COMMIT TX transfer
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] CUR3001 bal=300000
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] SAV2001 bal=950000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The point I like to make is that Spring and the JDK are not separate from design patterns; they are built out of them, so I am using patterns every day whether I name them or not. Recognizing where the framework uses a pattern is what proves I understand patterns practically rather than as textbook definitions.

In Spring, the container itself, the ApplicationContext and BeanFactory, is a Factory that creates and wires my beans, which is why I never call new on a service. Those beans are Singletons by default, one shared instance per container. Anything with @Transactional, and AOP in general, works through a dynamic Proxy that wraps my method to begin and commit the transaction. The template classes like JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, and JmsTemplate are Template Method: they own the fixed skeleton of connect, execute, and clean up, and let me plug in the one varying step through a callback like a RowMapper. Events use the Observer pattern through ApplicationEvent and @EventListener, pluggable AuthenticationProviders and Resource loaders are Strategy, BeanPostProcessor is a Decorator, HandlerAdapter is an Adapter, and UriComponentsBuilder is a Builder.

In the JDK the same thing holds. Every collection hands back an Iterator, which is the Iterator pattern. Comparator is the cleanest Strategy in the whole language because it lets me swap the comparison algorithm into a fixed sort. The java.io streams are the canonical Decorator, where a BufferedReader wraps an InputStreamReader which wraps a FileInputStream, each layer adding behavior. And Runnable and Callable are Command objects, an action packaged as an object to be executed later.

Why this matters in my work at the National Bank of India is very concrete. Knowing that @Transactional is a proxy explains a real bug class: if I call a transactional method from another method in the same class, the call does not go through the proxy, so the transaction silently never starts. Knowing the container is a Factory and beans are singletons tells me to keep services stateless. And knowing events are Observer lets me add a new audit or notification reaction by adding a listener without ever touching the transfer logic. So when an interviewer asks this, I am really showing that I read frameworks fluently and can reason about their behavior from the patterns underneath.
